Through the easy laughter she consumed, she slowly learned to laugh without fear or embarrassment.

That daily exposure helped free her from the constraints of a certain cultural and religious pressure she never knew how to name, but which had kept her enclosed within herself, distant from her own body and her own nature.

I cannot say exactly when I first saw her laugh openly. But I remember her last laugh. It was in hospital, when I asked whether the hotel service was good enough for her requirements. It was not a good joke, I know, but it was enough to make her laugh. And laugh she did – without embarrassment, without covering her face, without fear of dying.

item.title: The longest walk
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
How Father Michael Shanahan reconciled his identity with the Catholic Church’s position on homosexuality

- Directed by John Haley

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: For Father Michael Shanahan, coming out as gay occurred slowly, over decades. The process began with recognising a tension in himself, continued with confiding in his immediate family, and culminated in openly identifying as a gay Catholic priest. In The Longest Walk, Shanahan shares this story, including how, in the depths of prayer, he handled the conflict between his calling to the priesthood and the Catholic Church’s official position that homosexual attraction is an ‘objective disorder’ – a crisis that required its own leap of faith to resolve. Combining archival imagery from Shanahan’s life and contemporary footage of him conducting mass in Chicago, the US director John Haley forms a spare yet complex meditation on identity and belief.

item.title: Impatience is an emotion, not a trait
item.dc:creator: Amy Arthur
item.description:
Watching Penelope’s heroic wait in The Odyssey made me lament my impatience. But maybe I’ve been thinking about it wrong

- by Amy Arthur

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Last month, while watching Christopher Nolan’s new epic The Odyssey, I couldn’t help but marvel at the patience of Penelope, who waits 20 years for her husband – the king, Odysseus – to return to Ithaca. Despite no indication of when, or if, he might return, she is steadfast in her wait.

I cannot claim such patience. My husband has never left me to manage a kingdom, but I’ve been plagued by plenty of frustrating waits. I am as impatient about small delays, like queueing at the post office, as I am about the longer, life-altering ones. I remember how exasperated I felt by the multiple delays in moving to our first home, not to mention my impatience now at waiting nine years for an endometriosis diagnosis.

I’ve long assumed that impatience is simply part of my personality. But I recently came across a different perspective: according to the psychologist Kate Sweeny and her colleagues at the University of California, Riverside, impatience is not a fixed facet of who we are. Instead, it’s an emotion – and patience is the process by which we manage it. While this isn’t a novel theory, Sweeny’s team tested it recently with promising results – they found, for instance, that it’s not so much the length of the wait that matters, but how fair we consider it to be.

I find the implications hopeful. Just as we can learn to handle other unpleasant emotions, we can all develop better skills and techniques to deal with impatience.

As with other difficult emotions, one key to regulating impatience is likely to be acknowledging it in the first place. We see this in Penelope: she allows herself to feel the impatience, but finds a way through it. The next time I’m faced with a long delay, I’ll channel my inner Greek queen and know that it’s an emotion I can manage, even if I can’t control the wait itself.

item.title: How to be a word detective
item.dc:creator: Danny Bate
item.description:
Etymology unravels the mysteries of language and the hidden webs that link people across the world. Here’s how to dive in

- by Danny Bate

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
If I told you that there’s an activity that improves your vocabulary, your communication skills, and your knowledge of history and foreign languages; that provides an endless supply of fun facts and enjoyable epiphanies; and that is completely free and ready for you to start right this second, you’d be forgiven for raising an eyebrow of incredulity. But no, this multi-advantageous activity really does exist. I’ve devoted a significant chunk of my adult life to pursuing it.

In order to understand the words that your eyes are currently scanning, you first had to learn them from someone else – most likely from parents, older siblings, grandparents, teachers and others around you. Those people acquired their vocabulary from others still, and those others were instructed themselves. With this fact in mind, we appreciate that each of us is a link in a millennia-long chain of language, connected to people over the centuries by the words they bequeathed us. Following where, and through whom, that chain has passed is the business of etymology.

Like examining one fine thread of a spider’s web, tracking a single word’s etymology back in time will lead you into a web of connections between languages, peoples and places. In English etymology, my main focus here, the cast of characters is diverse. Legions of Romans, longships of Vikings, schools of Muslim scientists, academies of Greeks, and one fateful army of Normans in 1066 have all influenced the words of what linguists call Modern English (c1500 CE-present day). Of course, all those people didn’t exist in a vacuum. The whistling arrows at the Battle of Hastings and the scratching quills of William Shakespeare formed part of real historical events and sociopolitical circumstances that are still reflected in our vocabulary.

Etymology is therefore a great way to get stuck into the past, and many of us delight in history for its own sake. But that’s just one of the diverse benefits of becoming a word detective – learning to uncover the backstories of the words you use.

The delights of etymology

Most immediately, there are the fun bits of trivia and joyful ‘Aha!’ moments of realisation. These can come in handy in various social scenarios. That an aftermath is nothing mathematical but rather an ‘after-mowing’, that malaria is literally the medically outdated idea of ‘bad air’, that a migraine was originally conceived of as suffering a ‘half-head’ (hēmikranía) of pain, according to the Greeks, or that a dandelion is a French ‘tooth-of-lion’ are etymological titbits that might help a conversation flow, or win you that quiz night.

Etymology elucidates seemingly strange features of the English language. If we consider only the present, it’s baffling that a date is a fruit as well as a point in the calendar, and that a seal of approval isn’t the one with flippers (probably). Bring in history, and we gain soothing explanations for how this all came to be.

Then there are the linguistic skills that etymology nurtures, often subtly and incrementally. So many ingredients have been mixed into the English lexicon that sifting through them will naturally expose you to a lot of other languages – a heavy measure of French, several tablespoons of Latin and Greek, some Spanish for spice, a pinch of Persian, a dose of Dutch and a dram of Modern German. The etymology of one language quickly becomes a springboard for jumping into others.

The etymologist’s toolkit also includes the materials for word-building: prefixes, suffixes, roots. From these, the ancients constructed vocabulary. The Romans, for example, used via (the Latin word for ‘road’) as a root for coining what would become English devious, impervious, obvious, previous and trivial too. One Latin prefix, con-, unites concept, connect, constructed, continue, conversation and countless more.

With these conceptual tools, the vocabulary of English (or any language) is broken down and becomes more learnable – no longer an impenetrable mass of words, but an assemblage of recognisable basic elements. This can improve your passive knowledge of a language, but also your active creativity when wielding it.

Before we get started, consider some bigger-picture benefits too. I don’t exaggerate when I say that etymology can make people better at thinking about and interacting with our fellow humans. The etymologist accesses a unique perspective on human history. Language links faraway people and places in ways that aren’t generally known about. They can make the exotic feel familiar, and the domestic feel strange. When your language leads you to consider your small place in a world-spanning web of connections and an endless flow of linguistic innovation and conversation, it opens the door to cultivating humility, respect and kindness.

I believe that all this treasure is yours for the taking, stored in the words you already know. Now, I must admit that no one can teach you all the etymological knowledge in a short amount of time. It takes years to get up to the level of the expert word nerds – but the joy is in the journey. What I can do is get you started. The following steps will help you begin to think like an etymologist and see your words anew.

item.title: Town square
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Complete with a retro diner, vintage cars and a classic movie theatre – step into a mini town built to spark memories

- Directed by Josh Izenberg

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Town Square recreates the Americana of the 1950s and early ’60s with touches like a vintage diner, a theatre screening classic films, period-appropriate shopfronts and much more. However, the facility in Chula Vista, California isn’t an attraction for nostalgia-seeking tourists, but an adult daycare centre for people with Alzheimer’s and dementia. The ambitious project is the brainchild of Scott Tarde, the CEO of Glenner Alzheimer’s Centers. As Tarde explains in this documentary, the ‘small city inside a warehouse’ was built around the principles of reminiscence therapy, which seeks to immerse those with dementia in a more familiar past rather than constantly making them readjust to a confusing and uncomfortable present.

The US director Josh Izenberg documents Town Square throughout its construction and opening in 2018, when its philosophy was put to the test. He also gains intimate access to the families who used the facility in its early days. Crafted with skill and empathy, his film captures the potential of reminiscence therapy to reduce suffering while remaining honest about the immense difficulties Alzheimer’s presents for both patients and caregivers.

item.title: Lessons from Wyatt Earp country
item.dc:creator: Zeno Franco
item.description:
How does a man show up for his community? I learned from an old farmer on the edge of the desert

- by Zeno Franco

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In my teens, my mother was finally able to buy a house. It was out on old Highway 38, the back way up the mountain to Big Bear. Mentone, California was the last transition between the Los Angeles basin and the Mount San Gorgonio wilderness. A long way from where I had grown up, just off Sunset Boulevard, looking out a bedroom window at the Hollywood sign.

In the mid-1980s and after two divorces, another difficult ending with an ex-boyfriend had pushed my mother away from the ‘city of angels’ to a place where the grammar of urban streets transitioned to orange groves under palms. Land here was sold with agricultural rights, water purchased by the acre-foot – the amount of water needed to flood one acre of land with one foot of water. Mail was often delivered in personal cars marked as rural letter-carriers.

The older lady selling the house had been the wife of the pastor at the Christian Love Fellowship church half a block down. The church had maybe 30 dusty parking spaces; her husband played the vibraphone, sang and gave the sermon there for decades. When she first showed the house, she spoke fondly of entertaining with her husband before he passed on. In a somewhat bemused way, she showed us the dust jacket of a record he had likely self-produced, called The Sweetest Music This Side of Heaven. It featured lesser-known hymns with titles like ‘That Old Rugged Hill’. The album struck me as a project undertaken in answer to the way time seemed to stretch out before you here at the edge of the desert.

An addition had been built onto the back of the house that was almost as big as the house itself: an all-purpose room for church parties, with a pass-through from the modest kitchen, allowing hot food to be served. From massive wooden beams, chandeliers fashioned from actual wagon wheels hung in this room, rings of lights styled like kerosene lanterns. I asked the pastor’s wife what the metal hooks were on the wall. Reaching back even before the time when she and her husband were young, she said that the original owner was a hunter. The walls had been adorned with bear and deer trophies from the mountain that stood 11,500 feet above us. On move-in day, as a welcome gift, she left a large zucchini bread on the top of the antique Wedgewood stove, with handwritten instructions for heating it in the side-by-side broiler. I got the sense that, after losing her husband, leaving the stove behind was one of the hardest parts of departure for her.

While packing and preparing to move, my mom hinted that she thought I should stop talking to my dad, not send the new address, that I could disappear. When I was very small, enough time had passed between contested visitations that I had forgotten for a moment what my father looked like. I could not let that happen again. I sent dad the new address.

A few months later, the pastor’s wife put the one-and-a-third-acre of vacant land that surrounded the house up for sale. Although she was worried about every penny, my mother was also concerned someone else would buy it and develop close to the house. She bought it ‘owner carry’ or what is sometimes called a land contract, sending a cheque directly to the pastor’s wife each month with no down payment. A long chain-link fence extended from the house to the next property, with a large double gate that was padlocked shut. Proud of the slowly growing set of keys I had, sometimes I would swing one of the gates out and just stand in the open field.

I realised for the first time how much I hadn’t been taught without my father around

But it was more land than my mother or I could manage: a few tumbled-down fruit trees, an ageing irrigation system. And lots of weeds. In the spring, the county started sending out notices for weed abatement as part of the fire control strategy at the edge of the foothills, prime wildfire country. I bought a gas-powered weed-eater, started trimming, and found the remnants of a cement foundation for a small building behind the big paddles of a Barbary fig cactus. The weeds went on forever. I didn’t do a good enough job. The county sent out a five-man team and used a bolt cutter to get through the padlock and chain on the gate. They recut the field and sent a bill.

I remember watching Charles Bronson in the movie Chino (1973), on a small colour TV my mother had just bought. A solitary horseman who took in a stray, a boy maybe 15, and taught him his trade. Bronson up in the saddle, carrying a Winchester lever-action carbine. His jaw set, tough, unyielding and alone. For several weeks after, I wanted a rifle. Somewhere around this time, a water pressure relief valve broke outside of the house. Down on my haunches, inspecting how a steady trickle was beginning to flow under a wall, I realised for the first time how much I hadn’t been taught without my father around. The realisation felt heavy, almost enough to take me to the ground.

After a few false starts, my mom got ahold of a farmer who said he could take care of the land. He arrived early in the morning, pulling a large flatbed truck off the highway, hauling a John Deere tractor. I opened both gates to the land out wide, slightly sheepish for not being able to handle the job on my own. The most adult thing I had done was get a new Master Lock for the chain that the county had cut through. The farmer was old; we talked for a few minutes, he shook my hand and then he backed the tractor off the truck. As the tractor passed the gate, he lowered a large disc-harrow attachment to the ground. I watched from the window from time to time as he made slow but steady progress across the field. Against the dust, just a red bandana drawn over his face.

For two hours, you could hear the discs ploughing clods of earth, kicking up stones. When he was done, we looked at the cleared land together, and with a gloved hand he pointed to a raised rectangular section of the crumbling foundation I had found. He said: ‘Must have been a trough there a long time ago. Maybe a livestock shed. This used to be horse land.’

It was quiet enough that you could hear the pod of a poppy burst

Over time, I came to realise that stories I had heard about Wyatt Earp riding through the passes nearby were not stories at all. It wasn’t a Western movie. The lawman had come through Mentone to visit his sister Adelia, bringing candy to her children in the late 1800s before settling in Vidal, California out on the Mojave range around the turn of the century.

In the early morning and late in the afternoon there would be a lot of traffic on Highway 38, maybe 30 feet from the front door. You’d hear the hollow whistle of offroad tyres coming down the hill, decelerating for the first stop sign in a long while. But midday, as the sun climbed higher, things would become still, completely silent. Nothing except tumbleweeds and the territorial call of a mockingbird. It was quiet enough that you could hear the pod of a poppy burst, scattering the seeds far away from the flower. Once in a while in those moments, I would look up toward the Santa Ana Wash, east toward the foothills, and see a wagon train in my mind.

Every year in the spring, and again in autumn if there was rain over the summer, there would be this cycle. The notice from the county, the call to the farmer, the flatbed pulling up – usually on a Saturday morning, when all his other work was done. Every time, he and I would shake hands and sit on a low stone wall for a few minutes, watch the traffic go by, and talk in an increasingly familiar way. He didn’t talk fast; I don’t even remember what we talked about any more – so many years have gone by. But everything he said was offered with a tone of respect. It didn’t matter that I was still barely a man. He never talked long, just long enough and then he would climb onto the tractor seat.

Over time, I came to see an alternative language – different from my early understanding of the punctuated relationship with my father – of what it was to be a man: enduring connection over a span of years, thoughtful predictability, and a quiet know-how. Somehow a departure from my notion as a teen, with a guiding hand there only occasionally on weekends, that the goal was a stony exterior, reserved and unreachable.

My mom ended up in a clinic and I worried that no one was looking in on her

I moved away. Twenty years went by. Occasionally, my mom would update me: ‘Harry Pattison was up here with the tractor, we talked for a few minutes.’ As she approached her end, it was a struggle to manage care for her across 2,000 miles: a day spent in airports to get home, a day or two on the ground to look in on her, and a flight back to my own little family and work. Maybe because of the health problems, she had become increasingly isolated over the years, her social circle shrunk to passing conversations with storekeepers or chatting at a small table with the manager of a Mexican restaurant she frequented.

Some years back, she got sick enough that she ended up in a clinic in the town over, a small city. I was worried I could not get back right away, that no one was looking in on her, and there was no one to really ask. But when I called, she said: ‘Harry Pattison and his wife came to see me here at the hospital yesterday. They were holding hands when they came in. It was a nice visit.’

item.title: Is it morally wrong to not take care of yourself?
item.dc:creator: Laura K Soter & Fan Yang
item.description:
The philosophical debate goes on. But our research on self-obligations suggests there’s a common, consequential view

- by Laura K Soter & Fan Yang

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever felt guilty for how you treated yourself? Maybe you promised yourself you would work towards some goal and you failed to do so, or you continued to feed yourself unhealthy food, or kept yourself sleep-deprived because you wouldn’t stop doomscrolling in bed. Of course, we all sometimes make unwise choices or do things that have bad consequences. But there’s another intriguing possibility: that, in some cases, we owed it to ourselves to treat ourselves better – in other words, that we have moral obligations to ourselves. So, do such self-obligations exist? Do we feel their pull in everyday life?

Perhaps surprisingly, there is little consensus on whether we have moral obligations to ourselves. Nearly everyone agrees, of course, that we have obligations to other people. Most of us have felt guilty at some point for how we treated someone else; guilt is, often, a sign that (we think) we’ve done something morally wrong. Such failures can be big (seriously injuring someone in a bar fight, or cheating on a spouse) or small (forgetting a promise to pick up someone from the airport, or saying something unkind). Indeed, it is widely thought that morality exists as a set of norms that govern our interactions with other people. But, because of this, the question of whether there are also moral norms about how we treat ourselves is much more controversial. Obligations to the self don’t sit well with many standard ways of thinking about the nature of morality.

Some theorists question whether there are any genuine obligations to the self, for several reasons. One is that morality has been described as a system that arises when there’s a need to coordinate the competing interests of different people. Thus, it’s possible that how we treat ourselves is not inherently a moral issue. This is a perspective that many psychologists studying morality have taken, including proponents of social domain theory, dyadic morality, and the cooperative theory of morality. A stronger version of this view is that it would be overreaching to think of morality as governing how people treat themselves, in light of essential values of personal liberty or autonomy. For instance, in Fatal Freedom (1999), the psychiatrist Thomas Szasz used this perspective to argue that even suicide is morally permissible.

Another kind of objection is that obligations to the self are conceptually incoherent – they make no sense. With many interpersonal obligations, the person who is owed something can release the one who owes them: if you promise to cook me dinner, I can simply waive your obligation by telling you I don’t need you to keep that promise. But if the person who’s owed something and the person who owes it are the same person, couldn’t I just release myself from any obligation I don’t want to fulfil? This is known as the ‘paradox of self-release’, and philosophers such as Marcus Singer have worried that this renders obligations to the self either impossible or trivial.

Despite these sceptical perspectives, other philosophers have defended obligations to the self as a central component of morality. Immanuel Kant, for instance, thought that the duty of self-respect was fundamental to moral life. He thought that it was wrong to treat oneself (or anyone else) as ‘a mere means’ to an end rather than an end in oneself – and on this basis, he thought such varied acts as suicide, masturbation, and even cutting one’s hair in order to sell it were morally wrong. Confucius thought that self-cultivation was a valuable moral end. And contemporary philosophers have defended a wide range of self-obligations, including pursuing self-knowledge, avoiding self-harm, cultivating one’s talents, resisting oppression, and keeping promises to oneself.

A person’s sense of moral obligation is an essential force driving their choices and behaviours. If ordinary people endorse the idea of self-obligations, it would suggest that theories of morality that focus only on obligations to others have missed an important component of this moral sense. Therefore, wherever the theorists land on these matters, there’s an important psychological question to be asked: do people think that there are moral obligations to the self?

We investigated this in a series of recent studies. We started by simply asking US adults (aged 18 to late 70s) whether they thought they had obligations to themselves, even in cases when their actions would not affect anyone else. More than 85 per cent of the people we asked said ‘yes’. When asked for examples of such obligations, they provided a wide range, especially concerning taking care of one’s mental and physical health, but also cultivating moral character or living up to religious commitments.

Avoiding self-harm or taking care of one’s mental health were seen as matters of obligation to the self

But showing that people really think there are obligations to the self takes more than that. There is some consensus among philosophers that an obligation has at least two essential features. First, it is non-optional. So, obligations to the self can’t simply be personal preferences about how to live our lives or treat ourselves: they are stronger than that, and they hold even if we don’t always want to fulfil them. Second, obligations are directed to a specific target. It’s not just that I owe the money I promised I’d repay; I owe it to the person who lent it to me. In the case of obligations to the self, the target of these obligations needs to be the self. This gets at a crucial distinction between obligations that are genuinely owed to the self, and those that are in some sense about the self but are ultimately owed to other people. Consider, for instance, a soccer player who promises her team she’ll get in shape; here, the obligation is about her own body, but it is owed to her teammates.

With this in mind, we tried to dig deeper and see whether people really differentiate obligations from mere preferences, and whether they truly see them as being owed to the self.

When we asked people to classify a wide range of self-directed acts, they identified some, like avoiding self-harm or taking care of one’s mental health or personal safety, as matters of obligation to the self, while acts like drinking tea or reading fiction were matters of personal preference. Importantly, they also explicitly judged that, in violating the obligations, a person did something wrong to themselves, not just to other people. Backing this up even more, we asked participants to imagine a totally isolated person living all by themselves – think of someone stranded like Robinson Crusoe – and people still judged that it was wrong for that person to fail to take care of themselves.

In terms of what rises to the level of self-obligation, our final studies suggest that harmfulness is a key factor: people judge acts that are highly harmful to the self to be matters of moral obligation, but acts that are not harmful are more likely to be seen as a matter of preference. Harm may not be the only distinguishing feature – we also found evidence that people think acts that inhibit one’s potential or change one’s true self can be matters of self-obligation – but these were less predictive than harm.

Together, these results suggest people think that it’s wrong if one fails to treat oneself in particular ways. This raises a variety of interesting questions. After all, it seems like such beliefs could have both good and bad consequences, depending on the context.

For instance, it’s well known that people find obligations motivating, feeling driven to fulfil them. Is this also the case for obligations to the self? That is, could thinking of something as a matter of what you morally owe to yourself provide the motivation to do things that might otherwise be difficult – such as exercising, taking care of yourself, or pursuing long-term goals? If so, that would be one way that moral self-obligations could be a positive psychological force.

The tendency to moralise self-care might risk making us more judgmental, and less empathetic

But there may also be risks that come along with moralisation. People are often harsh critics of those who fail to fulfil perceived obligations: blaming them, feeling anger or resentment towards them, and in some cases thinking they deserve to be punished. Do we also think this way about those who fail to fulfil self-obligations? If so, such reactions could, in some cases, have negative consequences.

For instance, many self-help or spiritual movements emphasise that you owe it to yourself to be the ‘best version of you’. Although this can be a valuable message in the right contexts, we might also worry that such messages can trade on the felt moral value of self-improvement – especially when failing to act in the ways advocated by any particular movement is accompanied by messages of blame, shame or guilt.

Moreover, we might worry about the consequences of perceiving the failure to take care of physical or mental health as the failure of a moral obligation. Various kinds of mental illnesses or addictions might be seen as involving, or resulting in, chronic failures of self-obligations. The tendency to moralise self-care might risk making us more judgmental, and less empathetic, towards people dealing with such challenges – or, if we face these challenges ourselves, turn us into our own harshest critic.

And what happens when an obligation to yourself conflicts with other moral obligations (either to yourself or to other people)? Even if we have genuine obligations to ourselves, are there conditions under which these obligations can be waived or overridden?

These are some of the rich questions that are ripe for both philosophical and psychological investigation – and also questions that each of us might encounter in our own lives. For now, we hope that our research brings into awareness a more encompassing view of obligation, one that many people seem to agree with, even if they’ve never stopped to reflect on it before. The self might be the one person that many of us prioritise or neglect without recognising that doing so could be a moral issue.

item.title: Absence of presence and presence of absence
item.dc:creator: Nigel Warburton
item.description:
Mindfulness experts teach us to be present in the moment. I suggest an antidote – a meditation that’s focused on absence

- by Nigel Warburton

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The absence of presence

Mindfulness experts tell us to be present and experience whatever is in front of us. Take a raisin, observe its wrinkles, smell it, taste it carefully in a conscious mode. This is supposed to be an antidote to the absence of presence so common in our age of digital distraction.

As an occasional exercise, I’m sure it’s fine; but I’m sceptical about it as a fundamental way of being. Humans evolved with selective conscious attention, ignoring noise, responding preconsciously to environments, projecting expectations onto them. We ignore the present and we go beyond the present. That serves us well. Imagine taking a ride in a taxi driven by a mindfulness enthusiast who is relishing the light glinting from the bumper of the car in front, the particular smell of the vanilla air freshener, refusing to think ahead…

If you really want to practise mindfulness despite the risk of becoming like that taxi driver, try this antidote: meditate on absence.

The presence of absence

In a passage near the beginning of Being and Nothingness (1943), Jean-Paul Sartre describes arriving late to meet his friend Pierre in a café. He looks around: there are people, tables, cigarette smoke, sounds, smells, colours, a ‘plenitude of being’. ‘I was expecting to see Pierre,’ he writes, ‘and my expectation has made Pierre’s absence happen as a real event.’ As he puts it, ‘Pierre absent haunts this café’.

Here’s the meditation. Sit quietly for 10 minutes. Focus on someone you care about and who you expected to be with you now, but isn’t. Let their absence haunt you. Recognise that the presence of this specific felt absence is an important aspect of who you are that colours so much. This is as much a part of your experience of the world as the wrinkles on a raisin. Acknowledge and relish that, then return to your mostly preconscious way of being.

item.title: Why you should try living without free will for two weeks
item.dc:creator: Tara-Lyn Camilleri
item.description:
Set aside the philosophical debates and act as if there is no free will. It leads to less blaming and better questions

- by Tara-Lyn Camilleri

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
You’re driving in heavy traffic when you hear the screech of tyres, followed by a thud. You glance to the lane beside you and see that a black sedan has just slammed into the back of a silver SUV.

At first, the explanation seems uncomplicated. Brakes constrain motion, but not enough to overcome the car’s momentum, and the collision causes damage. A leads to B. Cause and effect in its simplest form.

Then you notice the drivers.

From the black sedan, music still playing, steps a young man in a tailored suit. You notice the car is a new BMW. He checks his phone and then surveys the damage to his vehicle. In the silver SUV, a woman in her early 40s turns immediately to the back seat to check on two children. You notice the family stickers on the rear window, and her hair coming loose as she leans inside the car.

You are no longer tracing forces and distances, but interpreting people, and your thoughts start to race. As the search for causes becomes a search for blame, a further assumption settles in, that somewhere in this chain of events, someone could have chosen otherwise.

It was probably the BMW driver’s fault. He checked his phone and the damage to his car before he even thought about the other people. He was probably looking at his phone while driving. Reckless.

This way of thinking is not confined to road accidents. When someone is late, we assume they failed to manage their time. When someone struggles with addiction, we say they need more self-control. When a person gains weight, loses their temper or falls into debt, the explanation often arrives quickly: they could have chosen otherwise.

Across these situations, complex interactions of biological, psychological and environmental influences are replaced with a narrative about personal choice.

To break this habit, I suggest a small experiment. For two weeks, try living as though free will were not the most useful way to interpret behaviour. You don’t need to decide whether it exists. If you live as if there is no free will, blame is no longer the default; behaviour must instead be understood in terms of the conditions that produced it.

When someone says they believe in free will, they usually mean that, in a given set of circumstances, we all have the freedom to choose differently. But I take a deterministic view of behaviour: what we do emerges from our biological state at any given moment, and that state itself is the product of how our body and brain grew, including genetic influences (development), what’s happened to us until now (life experience), and the current immediate and wider situation (environment). Environmental influences matter because biological systems are plastic and change in response to them. Determinism need not imply fatalism – the idea that outcomes are fixed regardless of what we do. I agree we have agency, but I believe our will to act is itself shaped by biological and environmental causes rather than freely chosen.

I arrived at this position gradually through an unusual mix of experiences. I first studied psychology, later worked in addiction services and the technology sector, and eventually returned to academia to study biological anthropology and evolutionary biology, researching how conditions experienced in one generation can influence the next. Across these settings, I kept encountering the same pattern: behaviour made far more sense when understood as the product of interacting biological, developmental and environmental forces than as the result of free choice.

Illness eventually forced this lesson on me personally. After a parasite infection during primatology fieldwork left me chronically ill, effort and determination no longer reliably produced the outcomes I expected. The experience made it impossible to sustain the familiar idea that people simply choose how their lives unfold.

That perspective shift has been a revelation and it’s why I’m inviting you to try it for two weeks.

Why we believe in free will

Belief in free will endures because it provides a reassuring explanation for failure and misfortune. If people freely choose their actions, then failure, illness, addiction, poverty or harm can be traced back to personal weakness or flawed character. That narrative protects us from hopelessness: They failed because they didn’t work hard enough. That won’t happen to me because I’ll work harder.

The stronger the belief in free will, the more we overestimate the role of personal choice, and underestimate situational and historical factors, particularly when judging other people. Experimental research finds that people who endorse free will more strongly judge wrongdoing as morally blameworthy, and indicate stronger support for punitive measures like punishment and retribution.

If substance use is treated as a failure of self-control, the response is to expect abstinence through individual effort alone

Yet this is misguided because studies show that rehabilitative interventions are more effective when they take into account the situational conditions, past and present, that lead to offending (such as poor education and environmental instability) rather than simply increasing the severity of punishment.

Another consequence of strong free-will beliefs is poorer diagnosis of behavioural problems and the pursuit of the wrong remedies. Consider addiction treatment. If substance use is treated primarily as a failure of self-control, the response is to expect abstinence through individual effort alone. However, studies show that structured financial-incentive programmes, which change the situational conditions surrounding the behaviour, lead to greater improvements in abstinence rates compared with control groups. People’s behaviour changes, not because they suddenly ‘choose better’, but because the environment makes abstinence more likely.

But without free will, what’s the point?

Challenges to free will are often met with understandable anxiety, largely because of concerns about what might replace it. If no one could have chosen otherwise, nothing is anyone’s fault. This is what many fear as moral nihilism: the collapse of blame, responsibility and ethical judgment altogether. Or people imagine the alternative to free will is fatalism: If I couldn’t have chosen differently, nothing I do matters, so why try at all?

Some laboratory studies have found that when people are told their behaviour is entirely predetermined in a way likely to engender fatalist beliefs (ie, it is the inevitable output of brain mechanisms over which they have no influence), they become more likely to cheat or exert less effort in short-term tasks.

This is why I want to be clear about what could replace free will. I’m not endorsing fatalism, but rather an evidence-based view of how our behaviour actually emerges.

I believe we are constrained but not powerless. Exercising agency doesn’t require us to be free agents

Across neuroscience and behavioural science, human behaviour is consistently shown to emerge from interacting biological and environmental factors: genetics, development, stress, trauma, resources, norms and history. None of this implies that our future is inevitable.

Because our biological systems are plastic, when inputs change, behaviour can change. Evidence-based interventions work precisely because behaviour is responsive to conditions. For example, children raised in disadvantaged environments show better developmental, educational and later-life outcomes when early caregiving and learning conditions improve. The constraints remain, but the probabilities change.

Although I don’t believe we have free will, I do believe we’re agents capable of influencing each other and the world around us, albeit that our agency is itself determined. We are constrained but not powerless. A person trying to quit smoking is not independent of cravings, stress or addiction history. But when the environment changes – through support, medication and reduced stress – different outcomes become more likely. Exercising agency does not require us to be free agents.

Letting go of free will doesn’t mean abandoning responsibility, nor should it excuse harm. But it can help us more accurately determine what went wrong when harm occurs. Instead of asking who deserves the blame, the questions become What produced this outcome? and What would make a different outcome more likely next time?

Return to the crash scene for a moment. The explanation that first formed in your mind might have been quick and simple – the BMW driver was careless.

But once you start asking what produced the behaviour, the picture becomes more nuanced. The BMW driver’s hormones and attention may have been compromised by a night of broken sleep. The glance at the phone might have been a message from a spouse updating him about the infant who kept them both awake. Or it might have been a demand from a micromanaging boss expecting an immediate reply. The car itself might not even be his, but a company car tied to a job where vehicle damage has consequences for his livelihood.

None of this removes the damage done to the SUV or the risk to the children in the back seat. But it does change our perception of the driver, and the explanation for the crash. What first appeared as a simple failure of personal choice begins to look more like the convergence of biological states, social pressures and the wider circumstances surrounding him.

When I stopped living as though I had free will

I had rejected free will intellectually long before I stopped living as though it were true. My scientific training had already convinced me that behaviour emerges from layered biological and environmental influences rather than isolated acts of choice. But like most people, I still carried the cultural habits of free-will thinking: the assumption that effort should reliably produce outcomes, that persistence should eventually bend circumstances to our will.

Chronic illness made that assumption difficult to maintain. The more I pushed, the worse I often became. Some days effort helped, but other days it triggered setbacks from which it took me weeks to recover. The familiar bootstrap narrative – that grit guarantees progress – turned out to be an application of free-will thinking to a system that couldn’t respond differently. Try as I might, I cannot just choose a well body. My agency has not disappeared but is narrower.

My experience exposed to me most clearly how readily we turn real limits into moral judgments and blame ourselves or one another, even for things like illness. Once you see the limits of free-will narratives in your own body like this, the broader cultural patterns become difficult to ignore. Again and again, we overestimate choice and willpower, and underestimate conditions.

I’m no longer making judgments and decisions from default blame and threat-detection mode

Dropping free will didn’t make me naive. I’m a survivor of deliberate cruelty. I’ve had boundaries ignored intentionally. I’ve also been harmed by people who meant well but lacked insight or capacity. The difference now is not that I excuse it – it is that I no longer stop at This is their fault.

When something harmful or unhelpful happens, I ask: What conditions produced this? What history, what stress, what incentives, what blind spots? Is this likely to change? Is this a pattern? The answers often calm me because I’m switching the parts of my brain I’m using, from blame to problem-solving – and that allows me to see more clearly.

Sometimes that clarity leads to empathy and compassion. Sometimes it leads to firmer boundaries. Sometimes it leads to distancing myself altogether. But I’m no longer making judgments and decisions from default blame and threat-detection mode. I’m making them based on available evidence.

Blame and anger have lessened, but they have not disappeared. Habits of moral judgment reassert themselves easily. I do the exercise I’m asking you to do each day, and I do it imperfectly.

Try it for two weeks

Living without free will for two weeks doesn’t require denying harm, injustice or accountability. It means changing the questions you ask. You don’t have to settle the philosophical debate about free will or determinism to try this. For two weeks, simply treat behaviour as something produced by conditions rather than pure choice.

When something goes wrong, replace Who is at fault? with What produced this outcome?

This becomes harder when the stakes rise, because blame feels protective. Especially in periods of instability or threat, certainty is comforting. Free-will narratives offer that certainty: someone chose badly, and that explains everything.

But try interrupting that reflex. See what happens when you delay the verdict and look for causes instead. If your experience is anything like mine, you’ll find that letting go of free will, even temporarily, makes room for something more useful: more accurate problem-solving, attention to causes, less shame, blame and reactive anger, and a clearer sense of where agency actually lies.
